lead: A VR or AR system cannot see, balance or respond without sensing. Sensors convert one physical quantity — acceleration, angular rate, magnetic field, light, distance or touch — into an electrical signal. Each sensor has a unit, a noise level, a bias and a drift, and the system combines several because no single sensor is enough. The same parts sit in a headset, a phone and a controller. This chapter groups them by what they measure and shows where each error comes from, so later tracker designs make sense.
prereq: You need the tracker view from Chapter 2.2; this chapter opens those trackers and looks at the sensors inside.

sections.h3: Inertial sensors: acceleration, rotation and heading

blocks.text: An accelerometer measures specific force along one axis. Specific force is the non-gravitational force per unit mass, so a stationary sensor reads g pointing up, not zero. Unit: m/s². A phone lying flat reads about 9.81 m/s² on its z axis, while free fall reads 0.
A gyroscope measures angular rate about one axis. Unit: rad/s or °/s. It gives fast rotation but has a bias: a small non-zero reading when still. Integrating rate gives angle, and bias adds up.

blocks.where: b_g is the gyroscope bias in degrees per second, t is the integration time in seconds, and θ_drift is the angle error in degrees.

blocks.text: A magnetometer measures the local magnetic field vector. Unit: microtesla, µT. Its direction gives an absolute heading, but steel, motors, speakers and desks distort the field, so the heading error can be large yet does not grow with time.

Dead reckoning means integrating rates and accelerations to update pose. Small errors add, so an unaided inertial sensor drifts. Fusion fixes this: a complementary filter or Kalman filter blends short-term gyro data with absolute gravity from the accelerometer and heading from the magnetometer. Head tracking uses this in Chapter 2.7.
Inside a headset the IMU sits rigidly near the front or side; inside a phone it sits on the main board.

sections.h3: Cameras and depth sensors: light and distance

blocks.text: An RGB camera measures visible light falling on a grid. Unit: pixel counts, later converted to colour. It supplies rich texture but suffers rolling shutter: rows are exposed one after another, so fast head motion skews the image. Auto-exposure changes brightness between frames. An IR camera sees a scene lit by infrared LEDs; it works in dim light but is affected by sunlight and reflective surfaces.
A depth sensor reports distance from the device to a surface. Unit: metres. Three common designs:

items: Structured light: projects an IR pattern and measures how the pattern shifts; error rises on shiny, dark or distant surfaces.
Time of flight (ToF): measures round-trip time of light, d = c t / 2, where c is speed of light and t is round-trip time; error rises in bright sunlight and at edges.
Stereo: matches two camera views and uses disparity; error rises on textureless walls.

blocks.text: In a headset, cameras sit on the front face and look outward at the world. These cameras support inside-out tracking: the headset works out its own pose from what it sees. Outside-in tracking is the opposite arrangement, where fixed external cameras or base stations look at the headset and its controllers. Eye cameras sit inside the headset near the lenses. In a phone, cameras are on the back and front. These sensors feed tracking, but marker and markerless tracking and SLAM are Unit 6.

sections.h3: Environmental and body sensors: contact and the user

blocks.text: These sensors measure the user or the surface they touch. Each has a unit and a dominant error:

items: Capacitive touch measures change in capacitance, in farads (F); error comes from sweat, gloves and contact area. It sits in controllers, touchpads and phones.
Flex sensor measures bend as a resistance change, often read in ohms (Ω) or mapped to angle; error comes from repeated bending and fit. It sits in gloves.
Force and pressure sensors measure newtons (N) or pascals (Pa); error comes from creep and placement. They sit under buttons, grips and shoe insoles.
Temperature sensors measure °C; error comes from self-heating and slow response. They sit in headsets to watch heat.
EMG measures muscle electrical activity in microvolts (µV); error comes from skin preparation, sweat and crosstalk. It sits on the forearm in research bands.

blocks.text: Gaze tracking uses pupil-centre corneal reflection. An IR light makes a bright corneal spot on the eye. An eye camera finds the pupil centre and the corneal spot, and the system tracks the vector between them. That vector shifts with head position and with each person's eye geometry, so on its own it is not gaze direction. After a short calibration for that user, the system maps the vector to gaze direction, reported in degrees. Error comes from glasses, dry eyes and headset slip. It sits inside the headset near each eye.

examples.question: A headset at rest reads a_z = 8.50 m/s² on the axis pointing up, with g = 9.81 m/s². (a) What tilt angle does that imply? (b) The gyroscope has a bias of 0.5° per second. How far does the integrated angle drift in 60 s? (c) A magnetometer heading is off by 10° because of a steel desk nearby; what happens to that error over time?
steps: For a static accelerometer, the measured specific force is the component of gravity along the axis: a_z = g cos θ.
Gyro bias integrates: θ_drift = b_g t = 0.5°/s × 60 s = 30.0°.
The magnetometer gives an absolute heading, so the 10° disturbance is not integrated; it stays 10.0° while the disturbance is present.
examples.answer: The tilt is about 29.9° (roughly 30°), the gyro-only angle drifts by 30.0° in 60 s, and the magnetometer heading error stays 10.0°.
examples.check:
import math
az = 8.50
g = 9.81
theta = math.degrees(math.acos(az/g))
drift = 0.5 * 60
mag = 10.0
print(f'{theta:.1f}')
print(f'{drift:.1f}')
print(f'{mag:.1f}')

traps: A stationary accelerometer does not read zero; it reads g pointing up.
Gyroscope bias integrates into a growing angle error, while accelerometer and magnetometer errors do not grow in the same way.
Unit slips: gyroscope in °/s or rad/s, accelerometer in m/s², magnetometer in µT, depth in metres.
Steel desks and motors disturb magnetic heading; do not trust a magnetometer indoors without a disturbance check.
Rolling shutter and auto-exposure corrupt camera features during fast head motion.

quiz.q: What does an accelerometer measure, and in what unit?
quiz.a: It measures specific force along an axis, including gravity, in m/s².

quiz.q: Why does a gyroscope-only orientation drift?
quiz.a: The gyro has a small bias when still; integrating rate adds that bias to angle every second, so the error grows with time.

quiz.q: A gyroscope has a bias of 0.2° per second. How much angle error builds up in 90 s?
Why does a magnetometer heading error stay roughly fixed while a gyro-only angle error grows?
quiz.a: The magnetometer gives an absolute reference each time, so a disturbance shifts the reading but is not accumulated. The gyro gives a rate that is integrated, so its bias is accumulated.

quiz.q: What quantity does a time-of-flight depth sensor measure, and in what unit is depth reported?
quiz.a: It measures the round-trip time of light; depth is reported in metres.

quiz.q: What is rolling shutter, and why does it matter in a VR headset?
quiz.a: Rows of the image are exposed one after another. Fast head motion skews the image between rows, which corrupts feature positions.

quiz.q: A capacitive touchpad reads 2.0 pF when touched and 1.2 pF when untouched. What change in capacitance does it detect?

beyond: Not for the exam. Production XR uses calibrated IMUs, camera-based visual-inertial odometry and factory calibration tables for bias and scale. Event cameras and on-chip fusion are active research because they cut latency and motion blur. Search terms: IMU calibration, Allan variance, visual-inertial odometry, structured-light calibration, pupil-centre corneal reflection.
